newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Violence flares in Central Africa, fear in Bangui.
newsitem.headline: Violence flares in Central Africa, fear in Bangui.

text.p: Hundreds of people fled the Central African Republic capital Bangui on Saturday following heavy fighting between mutinous soldiers and loyalist troops, witnesses said.
French warplanes stationed in the former colony flew over the tense city but French soldiers helping to patrol the city were not involved in the fighting, military sources said.
They said loyalist presidential guard soldiers appeared to be preparing for an offensive against mutineers who have controlled parts of the capital since the revolt began on November 16.
The exodus of people was mainly from the rebel-held southern and western districts of the city where residents fear attack.
"People are fleeing towards the south of the country which is under rebel control," said a resident in a district of the capital near the main road south.

There were no immediate reports of casualties in the firing which lasted for about four hours from 4 a.m. (0300 GMT) in one of the most serious exchanges since soldiers mutinied. Sporadic shooting continued by mid-morning.
French troops from France's 1,500-strong force in Bangui have been guarding the palace of President Ange-Felix Patasse and other strategic points under bilateral accords.
They fought bloody battles with local soldiers during a more serious revolt in May but have not clashed with the rebels since the start of the third army uprising in Bangui this year.
Rebel soldiers have hardened generalised grievances over pay and conditions and are now calling for Patasse's resignation.
"We demand the resignation of President Patasse and we are ready to put down our arms are soon as he leaves," a rebel spokesman, Sergeant Christian Guere, said.

Patasse, who was away in Europe when the mutiny erupted, returned home last Tuesday rejecting the rebel demand for his departure. He was expected to reaffirm his determination to stay in power in an address to the nation on Saturday night on the eve of National Day.
French troops in Central African Republic have been pivotal to France's numerous interventions in its former African colonies, notably Chad.

The bases played a key role in a French military mission to intervene in Rwanda in 1994. They are expected to be important in any French deployment to help refugees in eastern Zaire if the United Nations authorises a multinational force promoted by France.

Paris reinforced the Bangui base at the start of the current uprising, bringing the troop strength there to 1,500. But mutineers, who have demanded Patasse's dismissal, have warned the French not to use force to shore up the president.

Many ordinary people fear an outbreak of tribal violence in the impovershed country better known for the excesses of its former dictator Jean-Bedel Bokassa, who died last month. A planned state funeral has been held up by the mutiny.

The army is divided between soldiers from Patasse's northern region and militants from the south, suspected of allegiance to former president Andre Kolingba, one of several candidates defeated by Patasse in multiparty elections in 1993.
